lead_headline: Arvada Staff Showcases Bloomberg Harvard Innovation Work Across Four City Projects

type_specific.meeting_summary: Arvada City Council received an informal briefing on the city's participation in the Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Innovation Track, a free nine-month program that taught staff a structured innovation framework. Presenters from across city departments and the Arvada Economic Development Association described how they applied the methodology to four ongoing challenges: paid parking in Olde Town, homelessness response, the comprehensive plan community engagement process, and economic development partnerships. No votes were taken and no public comment was accepted.

briefings.topic: Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Innovation Track — Overview & Methodology
briefings.presenter_name: Dawn Cariela (name approximated from transcript as 'Miss Cara Ela' / 'Miss Kira Ewa')
briefings.presenter_role: Staff Lead for Innovation Program, City of Arvada
prose_paragraphs: The presenter walked council through the Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Initiative's (BHCLI) Innovation Track, a free nine-month program that the city joined at Mayor Simpson's invitation. The Arvada team included senior leaders Linda Haley and Brian Archer alongside the mayor, with a project team led by Mr. Wick and Jessica Garner. The program combined online learning with Harvard faculty, on-site team sessions, and two embedded coaches — a design coach and an innovation lead — to build structured problem-solving skills across the organization.

The program taught a six-phase innovation framework: setting an Ambitious Impactful Mission (AIM); researching affected residents and stakeholders; identifying root causes and systemic barriers; generating large volumes of possible solutions; tightening ideas into concepts; and prototyping minimum-viable solutions to test cheaply before committing significant resources. The team's own project focused on complex, emergent city-adjacent projects — using Quantum Commons as the test case — where the city is not the controlling party but residents still look to the city for answers. A central research insight was that residents want to be engaged collaboratively: 'do it with us, not to us.' Two prototypes emerged: a customer-service concierge role (already implemented through an existing staff position) and an evolved civics academy, 'Lead Where You Live,' which would give residents real policy case studies and feed their input back into city decision-making.

Post-program benefits have continued: the design coach provided additional hours on a homelessness project, the presenter received a scholarship to a Harvard Kennedy School executive education program in public leadership (completed the prior week), and the team joined an ongoing innovators network that includes a cohort from Des Moines, Iowa. The presenter identified three ongoing challenges for innovation at the city: staff capacity to execute new ideas, the reality that not every problem suits the innovation framework (some are process problems), and closing the feedback loop with residents so they know when their input was acted upon. The 'Lead Where You Live' civics academy prototype remains on pause pending a team member's return from parental leave, with a pilot targeted for later in 2026.

briefings.topic: Paid Parking Innovation Project — Olde Town Arvada
briefings.presenter_role: Staff Member, City of Arvada (presenting on behalf of herself and Kelly Van Bugen)
prose_paragraphs: Jacqueline Rhodess presented a 'sprint' application of the Bloomberg Harvard innovation framework to the city's ongoing paid parking challenges in Olde Town. The team's Ambitious Impactful Mission was to establish, by June 2026, a coordinated, in-house, sustainable paid parking model with consistent due process for Olde Town that improves access, supports local businesses, reduces congestion, and builds public transparency through clear policies and aligned operations. The sprint format allowed the team to move faster than the full innovation track, leveraging prior research studies and ongoing coordination with the Business Improvement District (BID).

The team conducted cross-departmental ideation sessions and generated more than 100 ideas. A key framing question that drove the work was: 'How might we ensure that paid parking feels like a tool for access and managing turnover, and not a barrier for customers and employees?' The presenter noted that the 'how might we' mindset has been particularly powerful in shifting how the team approaches problems. From the full portfolio of ideas generated, the team narrowed its focus to two prototypes: one centered on incentive programs to encourage visitors and businesses to use the parking hub, and one focused on improving the customer experience and physical wayfinding as visitors walk from the hub through Olde Town.

Both prototypes are in early setup stages, with sessions not yet completed at the time of the meeting. The presenter described the current phase as a low-cost model intended to test concepts with community and business partners before committing to full implementation. Additional follow-up studies are underway to inform the work. No specific timeline or cost figures were provided. The lead staff member on the project, Kelly Van Bugen, was not present at the meeting.

briefings.presenter_role: Staff Lead for Innovation Program, City of Arvada
prose_paragraphs: Immediately upon concluding the Bloomberg Harvard Innovation Track, the team launched a parallel innovation project focused on homelessness, utilizing post-program coaching hours with design coach Tim Fe. A city intern conducted research that summer reviewing successful approaches taken by other cities, with Columbus, Ohio highlighted as a model. Two ideation sessions were held — one with internal city staff and one with external service providers — generating more than 500 ideas. Those ideas were grouped into themes and then developed into actionable concepts using a prioritization matrix that weighed impact against feasibility.

Three concept posters were tested at community conversations: 'Common Ground Conversations' (structured community dialogue sessions around homelessness topics), a 'Bridge Team' (a group of community liaisons who would share information about the city's homelessness work directly with residents), and 'Activating Olde Town Square' (programming the square with public art, games, and varied seating to increase activity and perceived safety). Feedback from residents raised specific questions about the Bridge Team concept, particularly who the liaisons would be and whether they would be compensated. For the Olde Town activation concept, residents were shown images of different amenity options to gauge preferences. The Arvada Report newsletter was identified through the prioritization matrix as a high-value, low-effort tool worth continuing without further testing.

In a parallel track, the team convened a two-hour session with local faith leaders and facilitated a rapid innovation session — without labeling it as such — to identify how faith communities could support homelessness response. Three concepts emerged: a volunteer-matching website allowing people to find opportunities aligned with their interests; volunteer case managers from faith communities to walk alongside people exiting homelessness and provide community connection (distinct from professional case management); and expanded shelter options. Faith leaders were given concept poster templates to develop their ideas further and were scheduled to reconvene with city staff later that week. The presenter noted that a taxing district was identified as potentially high-impact but too difficult to prototype and was therefore set aside.

briefings.topic: Comprehensive Plan Community Engagement — Innovation Framework Integration
briefings.presenter_role: Staff Member, City of Arvada (Comprehensive Plan Project Lead)
prose_paragraphs: Jessica Garner described how the city is weaving innovation principles into its ongoing Comprehensive Plan process, which requires deep and sustained public engagement. Because the comprehensive plan process cannot follow the full Bloomberg Harvard innovation track sequentially, the team is taking a hybridized approach — embedding 'how might we' thinking, community storytelling, prototype-style feedback sessions, and problem-framing techniques into every public interaction. The goal is not just to gather opinions but to understand community challenges and convert them into design opportunities that ultimately show up as implementation commitments in the final plan.

Early engagement has focused on youth outreach, with sessions held at Arvada High School and Arvada West. Students told presenters that the questions being asked were not challenging enough and that they wanted deeper engagement; they also expressed frustration that their time with council during a prior lunch visit was too short. Themes from youth closely mirrored those raised by adults: housing affordability, safe and accessible transportation, and access to 'third spaces' for community gathering. The team also engaged more than 200 community members at the Kite Festival and plans to be present at Summerfest in early June.

Longer-term, staff expressed interest in establishing a youth advisory commission, describing current school engagement as planting seeds toward that goal. The presenter noted that sustained, consistent engagement over the next several years is expected to develop young leaders who will want to participate formally in city governance. No vote or formal action was requested; the presentation was intended to show council the early trajectory of the engagement strategy before the plan's core work is complete.

briefings.topic: Business Retention Innovation — AEDA Industry Roundtables
briefings.presenter_role: Staff Member, Arvada Economic Development Association (AEDA)
prose_paragraphs: Nancy Faulk presented on how the Arvada Economic Development Association (AEDA) applied the innovation framework to its business retention program. Facing the challenge that individual business visits are resource-intensive, AEDA piloted quarterly industry roundtables, beginning with beverage producers and retailers, as a way to connect with multiple businesses simultaneously. The initiative was framed around a shared challenge: how businesses can adapt to changing consumer habits. Participants generated ideas about AEDA program support and about ways businesses in the same industry could become more resilient by collaborating with one another.

Ideas from the roundtables are being clustered and prioritized using the impact-versus-difficulty matrix from the innovation framework, and AEDA is studying ways to develop programs that address the needs identified. The roundtables also produced an unexpected benefit: staff observed businesses forming strategic relationships in real time, including spontaneous conversations about product cross-collaborations and other joint resilience strategies that AEDA had not anticipated or planned for. These organic connections were described as a surprising and valuable immediate outcome of the format.

Faulk identified ongoing limitations: balancing the staff resources required to follow through on the needs surfaced in roundtables, addressing common themes that crossed both industries tested, and deciding whether to expand the roundtable model to additional industries. No specific budget figures, business counts, or implementation timelines were provided. The roundtable model itself is positioned as a more scalable complement to — not a replacement for — individual business visits.

briefings.topic: Economic Development Partnership Innovation — Aligned Network Project
briefings.presenter_role: Staff Lead for Innovation Program, City of Arvada (facilitator)
prose_paragraphs: The final example presented was a short innovation project focused on how the City of Arvada, AEDA, the Arvada Chamber of Commerce, AURA (the urban renewal authority), and Visit Arvada can better work together as an economic development ecosystem. The presenter facilitated the session and described the participating organizations as subjects of research for the project. The Ambitious Impactful Mission developed by the group was: 'By 2030, we'll have an aligned, high-performing network of economic development partners that make Arvada a world-class location for businesses and a community you want to call home.'

The session produced several actionable themes: improving how partner organizations share data with one another, since each currently holds different pieces of the economic picture; developing unified marketing and storytelling for the city as a whole rather than each organization promoting itself independently; strengthening coordination across the partner ecosystem; and building customer-focused problem-solving so that a business or resident is not told 'that's not my problem' but instead guided through the full system to a solution. The presenter noted that participants were creative but also pragmatic, wanting outcomes that were tangible and doable rather than aspirational.

The project is described as ongoing rather than concluded. No specific deliverables, timelines, or resource commitments were attached to the themes that emerged. The session was characterized as a beneficial initial experience that demonstrated how the innovation framework can be applied to inter-agency collaboration, not just internal city processes. Council was not asked to take any action.

questions_raised: Council Member Fifer indicated he felt the projects already underway were on the right track and asked for continued updates rather than adding new topics to the innovation portfolio.

Council Member Davis asked that staff coordinate internally so that questions raised separately by different council members can be combined and addressed together, avoiding duplicative or siloed responses.
Council Member Ambrose asked how innovation processes can be better aligned with the city's strategic plan and its resource-prioritization framework.

Council Member Lovisone asked how council itself can participate more creatively in study sessions and workshops — potentially using innovation tools like Post-it notes — so that discussions are more efficient and inclusive.

Mayor Simpson suggested that the city's ongoing infrastructure and roads conversation with residents could be a strong candidate for applying innovation practices, given its alignment with strategic plan priorities and wildly important goals.
